title: The Covenant in Moab and the Secret Things
summary: Moses calls all Israel, from leaders to foreign woodcutters, to enter the covenant the LORD is making with them in Moab, a covenant that includes generations not yet born. He recalls the exodus and the wilderness, warns against any person whose heart turns to other gods while imagining he will be safe, and describes future generations and foreign nations looking on a ruined land and asking why. The chapter ends by distinguishing the secret things that belong to God from the revealed things given to Israel to obey.
story: Deuteronomy began with Moses' first address (chapters 1-4), followed by the long second address containing the law (chapters 5-28). Chapter 29 opens the third address, which runs into chapter 30 and centers on the renewal of the covenant on the plains of Moab. The covenant made at Horeb (Sinai) forty years earlier is now renewed with a new generation about to enter the land. Moses reviews what God has done, calls the people to commit themselves, and then looks far ahead, past the curses of chapter 28, to the day when Israel will already be in exile and the nations will ask what happened. That forward look prepares for chapter 30, where the promise of return and a circumcised heart appears.
historical:
Verse 1 is numbered differently in Hebrew Bibles, where it is the last verse of chapter 28 (28:69), and the rest of the chapter is numbered one verse lower (so English 29:29 is Hebrew 29:28). Interpreters debate whether verse 1 is a closing summary of the preceding law or a heading for what follows; the English chapter division treats it as the latter.

The chapter recalls events told earlier in Deuteronomy and Numbers: the plagues in Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, and the defeat of Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan east of the Jordan, whose lands were given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Numbers 21 and 32; Deuteronomy 2-3). Verses 22-28 imagine a future in which the land lies ruined and Israel has been cast into another land. Those who date Deuteronomy late read these verses as reflecting the Babylonian exile (after 587 or 586 BC); those who hold to Mosaic origins read them as prophecy. The reference to Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim recalls the cities of the plain destroyed in Genesis 19 (Admah and Zeboiim are named with them in Genesis 10:19 and 14:2), whose region near the Dead Sea was remembered as a place of sulfur and salt.
cultural:
Covenant-making in the ancient world was a public ceremony in which all parties stood before witnesses and swore an oath. Verses 10-11 list everyone present: tribal leaders, elders, officials, men, women, children, and the foreigners who cut wood and drew water, the lowest laborers in the camp. Everyone is included, and everyone is bound. The covenant also extends to those who are not here today (verse 15), meaning future generations. In Israel's understanding, a child born later was already a party to the covenant made by his ancestors, and each generation stood where the first had stood.

The man of verse 19 invokes a blessing on himself, assuming that belonging to the covenant people will protect him even while he follows his own stubborn heart. Wormwood, the plant named in verse 18 (translated poisonous and bitter fruit), was known for its bitterness and became a common biblical image for the bitter results of sin. In the Masoretic text of verse 29 (Hebrew 29:28), the words for to us and to our children carry unusual dots above the letters, a scribal marking whose meaning ancient and modern interpreters have debated.
literary: The chapter is a covenant speech with a clear sequence. It begins with a historical prologue (verses 2-9), recalling God's acts as the basis of the relationship, which matches the pattern of ancient treaties. It moves to the covenant commitment itself (verses 10-15), with the repeated word today stressing that the covenant is present and binding. A warning follows (verses 16-21), and then an imagined future dialogue in which the nations ask why the land has been ruined and are answered (verses 22-28). The closing verse (29) is a short proverb-like statement that sums up the whole: some things God keeps to himself, but what he has revealed is given to be obeyed.

outline.t: The covenant in the land of Moab
What the LORD has done: Egypt, wilderness, and victory
All Israel, present and future, enters the covenant
Warning against a heart that turns away
Future generations ask why the land lies ruined
The secret things and the revealed things

doctrines.note: The covenant is renewed with a new generation and extended to those not yet born. It binds leaders and laborers, citizens and foreigners, and it rests on what God has already done for his people.

Verse 29 distinguishes the secret things that belong to God from the things he has revealed. Human beings are not given to know everything, but what God has made known is sufficient and is given for obedience across generations.

The danger the chapter names is the heart that turns away while assuming it is safe, a man who blesses himself and walks in stubbornness. Sin is shown as a root that spreads bitterness through a community.

words.note: Berit, covenant. A covenant was a binding relationship established by oath, with obligations and sanctions. The word appears seven times in this chapter. God's covenant with Israel at Horeb is here renewed in Moab, and the prophets later promise a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

Alah, oath or curse. The word refers to the sworn commitment that calls a curse down on oneself if the covenant is broken. Entering the covenant and its oath (verse 12) meant accepting the sanctions of chapter 28.

Lev, heart. In Hebrew thought the heart is the center of thought, will, and loyalty, not only feeling. Verse 4 says God has not yet given Israel a heart to understand, and verse 18 warns against a heart that turns away, preparing for the promise in 30:6 that God will circumcise their hearts.

Satar, to hide or conceal. The secret things of verse 29 are things God has hidden, his purposes that are not revealed. The verse does not forbid humble inquiry, but it sets the priority on obeying what God has made known.

christ: Verse 4 is quoted by Paul in Romans 11:8, joined with Isaiah 29:10, to explain Israel's partial hardening toward the gospel: God gave them eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear. Jesus asked his own disciples whether they had eyes but failed to see (Mark 8:18). The chapter's honest admission that Israel still lacked an understanding heart prepares for the new covenant promise that God would write his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), which the New Testament applies to the covenant inaugurated by Jesus' blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8-12). Hebrews also warns against any root of bitterness springing up to cause trouble (Hebrews 12:15), language that draws on verse 18. The covenant made with those not here today finds a Christian echo in Peter's words that the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off (Acts 2:39).

hard.q: If the LORD had not given Israel a heart to understand, how could Israel be blamed for not obeying?
hard.a:
Verse 4 says plainly that to this day the LORD had not given Israel a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear, even though they had witnessed his great works. Yet the chapter goes on to hold Israel responsible for turning away. The tension between God's sovereignty and human responsibility runs through the whole Bible, and traditions resolve it differently.

Reformed interpreters tend to read the verse as showing that spiritual understanding is God's gift, which he gives freely and is not obliged to give, while people remain responsible for the sin that flows from their own hearts. Wesleyan and Arminian interpreters tend to read it as describing Israel's persistent hardness, which God has not yet overcome because they have resisted, not as a decree that made obedience impossible. Many readers across traditions note that the verse functions as a confession of need, looking forward to 30:6, where God promises to circumcise their hearts so that they may love him. The chapter holds both truths without explaining how they fit, and verse 29 may be its own comment: some things belong to God, and what is revealed is given to obey.

questions: Israel had seen God's great works and still lacked a heart to understand. What have you witnessed of God that you have not yet taken to heart?
The covenant included the foreign woodcutter and children not yet born. What does it mean for you to be part of a promise made long before you arrived?
Verse 29 separates the secret things from the revealed things. Which unanswered questions do you need to leave with God, and what revealed things do you need to obey today?
